summary: This is an April Fools' Day RFC. It humorously proposes that routing area documents include a morality section, claiming that neglecting morality has led to a decline in moral values on the Internet. It is a joke and not a serious requirement.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC satirizes document requirements by proposing a morality section for routing drafts. Its required topics and examples use exaggerated and deliberately absurd claims.

subtitle: An April 1st satire proposing morality sections in routing drafts.

tldr.problem: The RFC's satirical premise is that routing protocols have neglected morality and harmed the Internet's moral values.
tldr.mechanism: It pretends to require a prominent Morality Considerations section in routing-area Internet-Drafts, with subsections on misuse, oversight, and other topics.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4041 is an April 1st joke, not a real requirement for routing documents.

today: RFC 4041 is an April 1st joke document. The unit metadata lists it as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Satirical Requirement
sections.content:
RFC 4041 is an April 1st joke presented as a serious process document. It claims that routing-area protocols have neglected morality and proposes that every new routing-area Internet-Draft include a Morality Considerations section.

The memo imitates formal requirement language while making implausible claims about the Internet and moral decline. Its apparent seriousness is part of the satire.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC pretends that routing drafts need to discuss moral effects. The proposal is satire, not a genuine IETF requirement.

sections.title: The Required Subsections
sections.content:
The proposed section must discuss misuse by supposedly depraved or misguided individuals, misuse by corporations, oversight facilities, inter-SDO impact, and care for avian carriers. The memo says even a topic considered irrelevant must still appear with a rebuttal.

It also jokes that encryption and obfuscation should be excluded so oversight can inspect activity, and includes a line about a duck being somebody's mother. These are satirical statements, not security or policy advice.
sections.plainLanguage: The listed topics turn document boilerplate into a series of exaggerated moral demands. The memo's claims should be read as jokes.

sections.title: Wordplay on Routing Terms
sections.content:
The applicability section applies moral judgments to service provision, political correctness, protection, and promiscuity. It makes puns about quality of service, jumbo packets, byte ordering, and multicast.

The terminology section defines routing and security terms through deliberately absurd explanations. Together these sections make network vocabulary the material for the RFC's humor.
sections.plainLanguage: The later sections make jokes by treating routing terms as moral or social questions. They do not add real requirements to those technologies.
